text: By the time I joined, Classeh's educational game was already live, sold to schools, stocked with content, doing its job. It wasn't broken. It was early: functional, but with clear room to grow.

text: A Game? Or a Table of Contents?
html: A Game? Or a Table of Contents?

text: Getting to a single game meant three separate decisions, made correctly, in order: subject, then chapter, then finally a list of games to choose from.
html: Getting to a single game meant three separate decisions, made correctly, in order: subject, then chapter, then finally a list of games to choose from.

text: That's not a game flow. That's a table of contents.
html: That's not a game flow. That's a table of contents.

text: The navigation had been built around how a curriculum is structured — not around how a kid decides what to play next. And every one of those three decisions was a place a kid could give up before reaching anything fun.
html: The navigation had been built around how a curriculum is structured — not around how a kid decides what to play next. And every one of those three decisions was a place a kid could give up before reaching anything fun.

text: Research wasn't yet a standard part of the process there, so I pulled together whatever signal I could get on my own.

text: I ran a lightweight heuristic evaluation against the existing flow, then handed the game to a few teenagers I knew -also part of our target audience- and watched how they actually moved through it, rather than how the flow assumed they would.
html: I ran a lightweight heuristic evaluation against the existing flow, then handed the game to a few teenagers I knew -also part of our target audience- and watched how they actually moved through it, rather than how the flow assumed they would.

text: Clarity's session recordings backed up what I was seeing live: kids lingering on the same screen far longer than a two-second menu should take, scrolling lessons back and forth as if they were re-checking something rather than choosing it. That's not what confident navigation looks like.
html: Clarity's session recordings backed up what I was seeing live: kids lingering on the same screen far longer than a two-second menu should take, scrolling lessons back and forth as if they were re-checking something rather than choosing it. That's not what confident navigation looks like.

text: Two things kept surfacing:
html: Two things kept surfacing:

text: — No intuitive flow: the path to play was a sequence of independent decisions, made correctly, in order, with no sense of progress in between

text: — Inconsistent visual language: pieces of the product didn't feel like they belonged together, which worked against the sense of immersion we wanted

text: Cutting the Decision, Not Simplifying It
html: Cutting the Decision, Not Simplifying It

text: Mapping the existing flow end-to-end surfaced something I hadn't expected:

text: this three-step decision sequence wasn't a one-time hurdle. It repeated multiple times in a single play session — and each repetition risked landing on a dead end.
html: this three-step decision sequence wasn't a one-time hurdle. It repeated multiple times in a single play session — and each repetition risked landing on a dead end.

text: The fix wasn't to make each decision easier. It was to remove the repeated decision-making altogether.
html: The fix wasn't to make each decision easier. It was to remove the repeated decision-making altogether.

text: I restructured the flow into a single, continuous path. Instead of subject → chapter → game list as three separate choices, progress became one line the user simply moves along.
html: I restructured the flow into a single, continuous path. Instead of subject → chapter → game list as three separate choices, progress became one line the user simply moves along.

text: INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE

text: Stepping on Backend's Turf
html: Stepping on Backend's Turf

text: The new flow needed a content structure to match. Different books had different numbers of lessons, and different content within them — so a fixed rule, like "two lessons per level," wouldn't hold. Lessons would drift out of sync with the school's actual schedule, reaching kids earlier or later than they were meant to.
html: The new flow needed a content structure to match. Different books had different numbers of lessons, and different content within them — so a fixed rule, like "two lessons per level," wouldn't hold. Lessons would drift out of sync with the school's actual schedule, reaching kids earlier or later than they were meant to.

text: My first instinct was to distribute content around the school's actual curriculum schedule, rather than how lessons happened to be grouped. But making that work meant restructuring the underlying database — and before refining the idea any further, I needed to know that was even possible.
html: My first instinct was to distribute content around the school's actual curriculum schedule, rather than how lessons happened to be grouped. But making that work meant restructuring the underlying database — and before refining the idea any further, I needed to know that was even possible.

text: I brought it to our CTO expecting pushback, or at best a scaled-down compromise. Instead, he told me to go ahead.
html: I brought it to our CTO expecting pushback, or at best a scaled-down compromise. Instead, he told me to go ahead.

text: That green light was what turned this from a UI exercise into a real structural project — and it's what let me take the idea from a rough direction to something concrete: schools followed a standardized lesson plan set by the Ministry of Education, dividing the year into fixed blocks. I mapped the roadmap to that same rhythm, splitting the year into segments of two and a half weeks each — matching a structure teachers were already following, rather than inventing a new one.
html: That green light was what turned this from a UI exercise into a real structural project — and it's what let me take the idea from a rough direction to something concrete: schools followed a standardized lesson plan set by the Ministry of Education, dividing the year into fixed blocks. I mapped the roadmap to that same rhythm, splitting the year into segments of two and a half weeks each — matching a structure teachers were already following, rather than inventing a new one.

text: TAKEAWAY
html: TAKEAWAY

text: Lesson Learned: Great Ideas Need the Whole Team
html: Lesson Learned: Great Ideas Need the Whole Team

text: The database restructuring wasn't rejected — the CTO backed it. But I didn't bring our backend developer into the process early enough. I designed the new flow and got it approved before looping him in, and by the time I needed to explain the new structure, it took real effort to get the idea across — he was confused by a structure he hadn't helped shape.
html: The database restructuring wasn't rejected — the CTO backed it. But I didn't bring our backend developer into the process early enough. I designed the new flow and got it approved before looping him in, and by the time I needed to explain the new structure, it took real effort to get the idea across — he was confused by a structure he hadn't helped shape.

text: If I ran this again, the backend developer would be in the room during ideation, not brought in after the flow was already decided. Not because the idea was wrong, but because a structural change like this needed someone who'd live with its technical consequences involved in choosing the structure — not just implementing it after the fact.
html: If I ran this again, the backend developer would be in the room during ideation, not brought in after the flow was already decided.
